topic: rebuilding a drystone retaining wall and repointing an older garden wall with lime mortar

provenance.author: CC (batch EN-1)
provenance.notes: napisane niezaleznie od korpusu PL, nie jest tlumaczeniem

base: I am rebuilding a drystone retaining wall that bulged badly after the wet autumn last year.
The older garden wall along the lane was built by the same hands and stands perfectly straight.
My wall leans outward from about knee height, though the foundation course looks sound enough.
Should I take it down to the ground, or only as far as the bulge reaches?
Take it down to the ground, because a bulge always begins lower than it appears.
Retaining walls fail through the hearting, the small stone packed behind the visible face.
If that packing has washed downward, the outer stones carry a load they never should.
Lay the stones out in rows as you strip them, keeping the largest for the base.
I stripped the wall right down and the hearting behind it had turned almost to gravel.
The older garden wall has proper hearting, as I found when a cap stone came loose.
I have relaid two courses with a firm batter and each stone touching its neighbours.
How much batter does a wall of this height actually need against wet ground behind?
About one part in six is usual, so a metre of height leans back sixteen centimetres.
Wet ground behind wants more batter and a drainage layer of clean stone against the soil.
Set every stone with its long axis running into the wall, never along the face.
Through stones at half height will tie the two faces together for the next century.
The wall is up to half height with through stones bedded across the whole thickness.
I have also started repointing the older garden wall, where the lime has gone powdery.
My first mix went off far too quickly and crumbled out of the joints within days.
Was the sand wrong, or did I simply work in weather that was too warm?
Warm weather is the likelier culprit, because lime needs slow drying to gain any strength.
Damp the joints well beforehand and cover the finished work with hessian for several days.
Sharp washed sand matters too, since soft builders sand leaves a weak and dusty joint.
Rake the old joints out properly first, at least twice as deep as they are wide.
I raked the joints deeper, damped them well and covered the work with wet hessian.
The new pointing has stayed firm for a fortnight and rings hard under a knuckle.
On the drystone wall I am now short of good coping stones for the top.
Can I set the copings in mortar, or does that defeat the point of drystone work?
Many good walls carry mortared copings, and on a retaining wall it is quite sensible.
The copings take the worst frost and the mortar stops children lifting them off.
Use the same lime mix and keep it well back from the visible outer face.
Set them on edge rather than flat, since an upright coping sheds water far better.
The copings are set on edge and bedded well back from the face as you said.
The whole wall is finished apart from backfilling the drainage layer behind the upper courses.
I have a heap of clean stone and about two barrows of coarse gravel left.
Should the gravel go against the wall, or against the bank of soil behind it?
Put the clean stone against the wall and the coarse gravel against the soil bank.
The graded layers stop fine soil washing forward and blocking the drainage over time.
Lay a strip of old turf upside down on top before you return the topsoil.
Then walk the whole length after every hard frost for the first two winters.
